## The idea

The top line of a bass staff is A3. The bottom line of a treble staff is E4.
Middle C sits in the gap between them, reachable by a ledger line from either
side. The two staves are windows onto one continuous pitch coordinate system.

The *bass clef* anchors F3 on its second line from the top. Relative to the middle
C coordinate from Lesson 38, the bottom bass line G2 is `-10` and the top line
A3 is `-2`. A *grand staff* joins bass and treble staves so low and high voices
can share a timeline. The clefs change the displayed window, not the underlying
pitch arithmetic.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 84

letters = [:c, :d, :e, :f, :g, :a, :b]
semitones = {c: 0, d: 2, e: 4, f: 5, g: 7, a: 9, b: 11}

define :staff_midi do |position, letters, semitones|
  letter = letters[position % 7]
  octave = 4 + (position / 7).floor
  12 * (octave + 1) + semitones[letter]
end

define :play_events do |events, synth_name|
  use_synth synth_name
  cursor = 0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], release: event[:duration] * 0.85,
      amp: event.fetch(:amp, 0.7)
    sleep event[:duration]
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

bass_positions = [-10, -8, -6, -5, -7, -9, -10, -7]
melody_positions = [2, 4, 5, 7, 6, 5, 4, 2]

bass = bass_positions.each_with_index.map do |position, index|
  {note: staff_midi(position, letters, semitones), start: index * 2,
   duration: 2, amp: 0.55}
end
melody = melody_positions.each_with_index.map do |position, index|
  {note: staff_midi(position, letters, semitones), start: index * 2,
   duration: 2, amp: 0.75}
end

in_thread { play_events bass, :fm }
play_events melody, :piano
```

The bass and melody occupy separate ranges and share sixteen beats. Their event
records use the same keys and their renderers start together. The coordinate
lists can be copied from two printed staves before either is translated into
MIDI.

## Change one thing

1. Move every bass position up seven diatonic steps. The notes rise one octave
   and begin to crowd the melody while preserving letter names.
2. Swap the synths. Register remains separated, but timbre changes which voice
   attracts attention.
3. Add a middle-C event at coordinate zero to both voices on the final beat.
   The identical MIDI value demonstrates that middle C belongs to the joined
   system rather than exclusively to one clef.

## Why it works

Both clefs call the same `staff_midi` function because position zero has already
been defined globally. Reading a bass note means measuring its diatonic offset
from middle C, exactly as for treble. A clef-specific implementation would add
an anchor offset and produce the same coordinate.

The grand staff is also a concurrency model. Bass and melody are independent
event arrays with one clock. `in_thread` starts one renderer while the main thread
runs the other. Shared starts prevent drift; separate data keeps editing one
voice from disturbing the other.

Keyboard notation often associates bass with the left hand and treble with the
right. Clef and hand are separate concepts. Either hand can cross the other, and
other instruments use either clef without a keyboard. The code names voices by
range instead of hand assignment.

The event timelines also make vertical alignment testable. Notes with equal
`:start` values sound together even when their source positions appear on
different staves. A barline gives both voices the same metric boundary. Before
playback, compare each voice's final start plus duration and reject a pair that
ends on different beats unless the score explicitly contains that asymmetry.

## Take it further

Encode an eight-bar two-voice sketch from a printed grand staff. Store the
original staff coordinate beside `:note`, `:start`, and `:duration` in every
event. Assert that both voices end at the same beat. Include one ledger-line note
in each clef and one shared middle C, then render the voices with contrasting
synths.
